subtype: Approach: thinks a task will take only a few minutes [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Yash. Before dinner I said, I'll finish this drawing in ten minutes. It was a big picture of a train station with lots of people. I did the platform first, then the train, then the little people, then the clouds. Then I looked at the clock and it had been one whole hour.
Mummy called, "Yash, dinner!" and I wasn't finished. I felt very upset and cross, and I said "Wait, wait!" too loudly. The drawing was still not done when I sat down, and my dinner was cold.
Next time I will not say ten minutes.

qa.q: How long did the drawing really take?
qa.a: The drawing took one whole hour.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when Mummy called for dinner?
qa.a: Yash felt very upset and cross, because the drawing was not finished.

qa.q: What could Yash do next time before promising a time?
qa.a: Yash could guess a time for each part, such as the platform and the train, and add them up, since the whole picture had many parts.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the loud 'Wait, wait!'?
qa.a: Mummy had made dinner and called kindly, so may feel a bit hurt or tired when the answer comes back too loudly.

grounding: A child expects to finish a drawing in ten minutes, it takes an hour, and Yash is upset when called for dinner.

Note from Vijay's mother, Devika, to his class teacher

Just so you know why his drawing homework is unfinished. Yesterday at 7:30 Vijay said, "I'll finish the forest drawing before dinner. Ten minutes." I said fine. At 7:40 he had drawn two trees and was colouring the sky. At 8:00 he was on the river. At 8:30 I called him for dinner, and he burst into tears, saying he hadn't finished and it was "ruined." He had never thought about how long each part would take. We talked afterwards, and he agreed that next time he will count the parts first: trees, river, sky, animals. He'll finish it this evening. Please don't mark him down; he is very upset about it.

qa.q: How long did Vijay say the drawing would take?
How did Vijay feel when his mother called him for dinner?
qa.a: He was very upset and frustrated, bursting into tears because it wasn't finished.

qa.q: What small step did Vijay agree to try next time?
qa.a: Counting the parts first, like trees, river, sky and animals, to see how long it will really take.

qa.q: How might the class teacher see this note?
qa.a: The teacher would likely understand and be gentle, seeing Vijay underestimated the time and is already upset.

grounding: A boy says he will finish a drawing in ten minutes before dinner, it takes an hour, and he is upset when his mother calls.

passage:
Tuesday

Today I told Mummy, "I'll finish my comic drawing in ten minutes, then I'll come for dinner." I thought ten minutes was loads. I drew the first box, a superhero cat. Then the second box, the cat flying. Then I needed the city under him, with buildings and windows, and that took forever. Nilesh, my little brother, kept asking if I was done. Then Mummy called, "Madhav, beta, dinner!" I looked at the clock and it had been an hour! I still had four boxes left. I got so cross I shouted, "You always call me at the wrong time!" That wasn't fair. It wasn't Mummy's fault. I just thought it would be quick. Next time I'll count the boxes first.

qa.q: How many boxes did Madhav still have left?
How did Madhav feel when Mummy called?
qa.a: He felt cross and frustrated, then guilty for shouting when it wasn't Mummy's fault.

qa.q: What could Madhav try before starting a drawing next time?
qa.a: Count the boxes first and guess how long each takes, as the diary plans, before promising a time.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when Madhav shouted?
qa.a: Mummy may have felt hurt or surprised, since she was only calling him for dinner.

grounding: A boy says he will finish his drawing in ten minutes before dinner, it takes an hour, and he gets upset when his mother calls.
